desc:
Cut nums into consecutive non-empty blocks (every element belongs to exactly one block, order preserved). The sum of each block must be at most cap. The cost of a split is the total of the maximum element of every block. Return the minimum possible cost.

Every element is at most cap, so a valid split always exists.

nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5], cap = 8
[3,1,4] [1,5]  -> blocks sums 8 and 6, cost 4 + 5 = 9
[3,1] [4,1] [5] -> cost 3 + 4 + 5 = 12
[3,1,4,1] [5]  -> sum 9 > 8, not allowed
[3] [1,4,1] [5] -> cost 3 + 4 + 5 = 12
result = 9
constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit integer (it is at most the sum of nums)
hints: Let dp[i] be the best cost for the first i elements. The last block is nums[j+1..i] for some j, so dp[i] = min(dp[j] + max(nums[j+1..i])) over the j whose block sum is within cap. That is O(n2).

Because all numbers are positive, dp is non-decreasing, and the smallest allowed j for each i never decreases. As i grows, the maximum of the last block takes only a few distinct values: the entries of a decreasing monotonic deque.

For a deque element k with predecessor p, all starts j in [p, k-1] have block maximum nums[k], and the best of them is j = p (dp is non-decreasing). Candidate: dp[p] + nums[k]. Keep the candidates in a min-heap with lazy deletion, plus handle the front element separately using the left boundary of the cap.
editorial: The dynamic program is dp[i] = min over j of dp[j] + max(nums[j+1..i]) for all j with sum(nums[j+1..i]) ≤ cap. The valid j form a window [L, i-1] whose left end L only moves right. Positive numbers make dp non-decreasing: dropping the last element of an optimal split of the first i+1 elements gives a valid split of the first i elements that costs no more.

Keep a deque of indices of strictly decreasing values (the suffix maxima of the current prefix). For deque element k with predecessor p, every start j in [p, k-1] sees block maximum nums[k], and by monotonicity the cheapest is j = p, giving candidate dp[p] + nums[k]. For the front element the lower bound is L instead of a predecessor, giving dp[L] + nums[front]. Candidates of non-front elements never change while the element is in the deque, so they sit in a min-heap with lazy deletion (skip entries whose element has left the deque or became the front).

Each index is pushed and popped at most once in the deque and the heap, so the total time is O(n log n) and the space O(n). A variant with a balanced multiset gives the same bounds; the simple O(n * cap) approach of scanning the window is the brute-force baseline.
solution:
def minBlockMaxTotal(nums, cap):
    from collections import deque
    import heapq
    n = len(nums)
    a = [0] + nums
    pref = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        pref[i] = pref[i - 1] + a[i]
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    alive = [False] * (n + 1)
    dq = deque()
    heap = []
    L = 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        while pref[i] - pref[L] > cap:
            L += 1
        while dq and a[dq[-1]] <= a[i]:
            alive[dq.pop()] = False
        if dq:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (dp[dq[-1]] + a[i], i))
        dq.append(i)
        alive[i] = True
        while dq[0] <= L:
            alive[dq.popleft()] = False
        front = dq[0]
        best = dp[L] + a[front]
        while heap and (not alive[heap[0][1]] or heap[0][1] == front):
            heapq.heappop(heap)
        if heap and heap[0][0] < best:
            best = heap[0][0]
        dp[i] = best
    return dp[n]
